author: nathan-hewitt
description: Between 1839 and 1860, Britain fought two wars against China to force on it a drug it had banned. Two victories for "free trade" that China remembers with bitterness.

hero.hook: A European power fought two wars to force a country to accept a drug it had banned.

blocks.text: Between **1839 and 1860**, Britain waged two wars against China to protect a drug trade. Its navy forced open Chinese ports and swept aside the empire's trade rules. The prize was [[opium]], a highly addictive substance made from the poppy plant, and one of the British Empire's most profitable goods.

These Opium Wars devastated China. British power shattered its self-confidence and subjected it to unequal treaties. Millions of Chinese became addicted to a drug that British guns had forced into their ports. For London, it was a victory for unfettered trade. For China, it was the start of a century of defeats and humiliations.

By the 1830s, relations between Britain and China were strained. The Chinese empire had never liked foreign traders: it confined all European commercial activity to the single port of [[Canton]], in the south of the country. The British, for their part, believed in [[free trade]], the idea that goods should move without barriers. They found these restrictions backward and insulting. They wanted Chinese goods, tea, porcelain. But China had little interest in buying anything from them.

With one exception: opium. The British grew thousands of tons of it every year in [[Bengal]], in eastern India. The crop was immensely profitable, but destructive: the drug was addictive and ruined the health of those who smoked it. The Chinese government had **banned it in 1796**. But corrupt officials and smugglers were willing to buy it in secret. The British slipped the chests into China beneath the emperor's notice. Or so they thought.

blocks.caption: The stacking room of the opium factory at Patna, in Bengal, around 1850: thousands of balls of opium bound for China.

sections.title: Canton, free trade and opium smuggling

blocks.text: By the late 1830s, smuggled opium was producing a massive addiction crisis in China. The emperor had to act. In **1839**, he sent a senior official, [[Lin Zexu]], to Canton with orders to stamp out the trade. Lin Zexu confiscated and destroyed thousands of chests of British opium. London saw it as an attack on its merchants and on free trade.

Lin Zexu is a hero in China today and an icon of the fight against drugs. June 26, the day he had the opium destroyed in 1839, has become the United Nations' International Day Against Drug Abuse and Illicit Trafficking.

The Royal Navy set sail with orders to force China open to British trade. The Chinese army, weak and poorly equipped, was no match for modern British firepower. In **1842**, China had to sign the humiliating [[Treaty of Nanking]]: it opened **five ports** to British trade and handed over Hong Kong. Opium remained officially banned, but China no longer had any way of stopping the British from smuggling it in.

blocks.caption: The signing of the Treaty of Nanking aboard the British warship HMS Cornwallis, August 29, 1842.

sections.title: Lin Zexu and the First Opium War

blocks.text: The opening of five ports was a windfall for the British, but it was not enough for them. Most of China remained closed to their ships, and the official ban on opium still stood. If those two locks could be broken, British merchants stood to make enormous profits. All that was missing was a pretext.

In **1856**, Chinese officials seized another shipment of British opium at Canton. London treated the affair as an attack on one of its ships and sent the fleet back. This time, French ships joined it: France wanted its own share of the China trade. The Second Opium War was another crushing defeat for China. The treaties that ended it effectively legalized the opium trade. China had to open more ports to foreign merchants and grant foreign nationals diplomatic and travel rights on its territory.

sections.title: The second war and the legalization of the trade

blocks.text: In the years that followed, the British flooded China with opium. Millions of people became addicted. Opium abuse remained one of the country's gravest social problems into the **20th century**. Meanwhile, Britain and the other foreign powers drew enormous profits from that misery.

blocks.caption: Opium smokers in a Chinese opium den, late 19th century.

blocks.text: The humiliating treaties imposed by Britain and its allies left a lasting mark. Later Chinese historians would see the Opium Wars as the start of a [[Century of Humiliation]] at the hands of foreign powers. To this day, these wars are a bitter memory in China. A memory that continues to shape its attitude toward any foreign interference in its affairs.

blocks.text: To protect the opium trade, Britain imposed "free trade" on China by force of arms, at the cost of millions of addicts and a century of humiliation whose memory still weighs today.
